sweep_summary: Japanese (nucl1643) is in the catalog as 'tonal' (lexical pitch accent) on Kawahara 2015 (held). Of 66 works with stress in the title, about 30 concern word accent of Tokyo/standard Japanese; the rest are phrasal prosody, other dialects (Kyoto, Kagoshima, Tsuruoka, Koshikijima), proto-Japanese reconstruction, or noise (L2 English accents, rakugo rhythm, palatal 'prosody'). Newly downloaded and read (all with record): McCawley 1965 MIT thesis (open on MIT DSpace), Shimabukuro 2002 UH dissertation (ScholarSpace), Poppe 2015 UTokyo dissertation, Kubozono 2006 Lingua (Kobe repository accepted MS), Ding 2006 (JUL open access), Kibe 2010 (NINJAL repository, Japanese), Ito & Mester 2007/2013/2019 (author copies), Seo et al. 2019 (ICPhS), plus an extra open find not in the list, Weitzman 1970 (USC/ONR instrumental study, ERIC). Every one describes Tokyo Japanese as a pitch accent system: at most one HL fall per word/phrase, lexically present-or-absent and lexically located (n+1 patterns), antepenultimate default in loanwords, F0 not intensity the correlate, no word stress. None contradicts or refines the classification beyond what the held Kawahara 2015 already states; the McCawley 1965 statement is the best new first-hand corroboration but does not supersede Kawahara 2015. Unread items that would deepen but not change the record: Kubozono 2011 (Blackwell), 2012 (Lingua), 2008 (Oxford Handbook) - all paywalled, medium priority; the remaining paywalled/print items (Haraguchi 1988, Nishiyama 2010, Oshima 2014, compound-accent papers, Yoshida 1995 thesis, Bostrom 1993, Kubozono 1993, Akinaga 1985) are low. discovery relied on Crossref, CiNii, Semantic Scholar, DSpace/WEKO APIs and archive.org (OpenAlex and Bing were unusable).

new_statements.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched.

The distinctive property of words is, then, the presence and location of the fall from high to low. [p.29] ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Tokyo Japanese has lexical pitch accent: the only distinctive word property is whether and where a high-to-low fall occurs; the initial low mora is predictable (first mora low unless the first syllable is heavy or the second mora is low). The tone-bearing unit is the mora but the accent domain is the syllable (in a heavy syllable the fall can only follow its first mora, p.35). No stress independent of pitch accent is normally recognised.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §1.5 (pp.42-49) discusses a possible non-contrastive 'stress system of sorts': a subjective impression of initial prominence on words (Hattori and Poser's consultants), phrase-final lengthening, and an alternating rhythm of bimoraic feet built left to right with the first mora of each foot stronger, whose 'principal if not only phonetic exponent is found in duration, not F0 or vowel quality' (p.43); Poser states no instrumental investigation had been made.
new_statements.exceptions: Words may be unaccented (no fall). Poser explicitly argues (p.42) that Hattori's prosodeme does not attribute non-tonal correlates to the accent itself.
new_statements.identity_note: Poser describes the Tokyo dialect (standard Japanese), as does the existing McCawley 1965 statement; Fon's Japanese subjects were Tokyo Japanese speakers from Tokyo and three neighbouring prefectures. No other variety is described in the opened works.

new_statements.quote: Theoretically, a lexical accent may land on any one of the vowels in a word. However, in Standard Japanese, if a word consists of three 'syllables (in traditional terms)' or less, the lexical accent location is random, unlike longer words whose accent location is predictable (Haraguchi 1991). Also, it is said that there is class of nouns without lexical accent. [...] Note that the pitch pattern is predictable if the location of the accent is known. [...] accent location in certain classes of words is predictable, and accordingly Standard Japanese should be regarded as any other stress system: to wit, the stress (accent) location is predictable, if it is not specified lexically.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (lexical pitch accent in Tokyo/Standard Japanese: presence vs absence and location of one accent, pitch contour predictable from it), so no contradiction; adds placement detail not in the Kawahara record or the McCawley/Poser statements: accent location is lexically free only in short nouns (<=3 OR pairs/moras: n+1 classes incl. unaccented), long morphologically simplex nouns and loanwords take default antepenultimate accent, short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless, the domain-initial nucleus is never high unless itself accented, and compound/verb/phrase accent is derived by the same principles; Yoshida treats the system formally as a stress system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard (Tokyo) Japanese is a lexical pitch accent language: a word has at most one accent (or none); from the accented nucleus leftwards all nuclei except the word-initial one are high, nothing after it is high, so the contour follows from the accent location. In nouns of up to three moras (OR pairs) the accent location (or its absence) is lexical (n+1 classes: na'mida, tama'go, takara', kuruma); morphologically simplex nouns of four or more OR pairs and long loanwords get default antepenultimate accent (mura'saki, hototo'gisu, suto'resu, puro'guramu), analysed as the head of the penultimate right-headed foot; short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless; compound, noun+particle, verb and sentence accent are derived from the members' lexical properties by the same licensing principles. The author argues the formalism is identical to stress assignment (predictable unless lexically specified).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None posited: only one head (accent) per domain; footnote 6 p.78 says only primary prominence is discussed. No stress independent of pitch accent is claimed anywhere in the thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked short nouns and some loans keep accent off the default site; final-accented and accentless nouns are homophonous in isolation and distinguished only before particles (-ga); 'devoiced' high vowels and the moraic nasal cannot bear accent, shifting it (sec. 3.3); genitive -no deaccents certain final-accented nouns (sec. 4.3.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Yoshida 1995 treats Standard (Tokyo) Japanese; Bostrom 1993 (title) treats Japanese pitch accent generally, presumably Tokyo standard; Otaka 2009 treats standard Japanese rhythm/timing (moras, feet, geminates); Hirata 2006 is Japanese syntax.

As can be seen in (1), the nominal accent system is an example of a system with n+1 patterns for nouns with n moras (or syllables). ... [p.21:] According to McCawley (1968), the default accent in Tokyo Japanese is placed on the syllable that contains the third mora from the right (see Chapter 3).
sources.note: Tokyo Japanese has lexical pitch accent with n+1 contrastive patterns (accent on any mora or unaccented); default/antepenultimate accent; the thesis reviews accentual vs tonal analyses (pp.16, 23) but nowhere posits stress. Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.quote: High tones are defined language-dependently. In English, high tones are pitch-accents that contain an H defined in the ToBI prosodic system promoted by Beckman and Ayers Elam (1997). [...] For Japanese, high tonal targets of pitch-accented syllables, which are always high, were chosen. [p.39] ... BI2 and BI3 represent accentual (AP) and intonational phrase (IP) disjunctures, respectively. [p.50]

Speakers were 'Tokyo Japanese from Tokyo and three neighboring prefecties' (methods, printed p.31). The MPG PuRe file is audience-restricted; the record's public OSU link was used.

sources.citation: Kibe, Nobuko (2010). Hogen akusento no tanjo [The formation of various accent systems in Japanese]. NINJAL Project Review 3, 23-35 (in Japanese, English abstract).
sources.quote: すでに多くの研究によって明らかにされているように，東京方言のアクセントは，＜下げ核があるかないか，あるとすればどの拍にあるか＞によって型の種類が区別される体系をもつ。無核の型を含めて，１拍語には２つの型，２拍語には３つの型，３拍語には４つの型，４拍語には５つの型，n 拍語には n＋１の型が存在することになる。 [Translation: As many studies have made clear, the accent of the Tokyo dialect is a system in which pattern types are distinguished by whether there is a fall-kernel (sage-kaku) and, if so, on which mora it lies. Including the kernel-less pattern, 1-mora words have 2 patterns, 2-mora words 3, 3-mora words 4, 4-mora words 5, and n-mora words n+1 patterns.]
sources.note: Primarily about the diachronic origin of dialect accent diversity, but gives a first-hand statement of the Tokyo system: accent = presence/location of a pitch-fall kernel, n+1 patterns. Confirms the tonal/pitch accent coding.

sources.citation: Ito, Junko and Mester, Armin (2007). Prosodic adjunction in Japanese compounds. MIT Working Papers in Linguistics 55 (FAJL 4), 97-111.
sources.quote: Comparison with the accentual patterns of the simplex words in (4) shows that not only does the accent of the first compound member disappear, but a junctural accent on the first syllable replaces whatever accent the second member has in isolation. ... the Japanese pitch accent is a head feature: Each accent must be the head of some minimal prosodic phrase. This ensures that every minimal [phrase] has at most one accent
sources.locator: p.3 of author copy (about p.99 of MITWPL 55), §2
sources.note: Compound accent: culminative pitch accent (at most one per minimal phrase), junctural accent at the left edge of the second member; contrasts this with English stress subordination. Confirms pitch accent coding; silent on simplex-word placement.

sources.quote: Since the size of the underlying domain is not fixed in standard Japanese, the number of types is open, ranging from Type-0 to Type-n in the table. Type-0 is usually regarded as 'unaccented', for the pattern does not have a pitch fall. ... In all other types, the number in the type name signifies the locus of the H tone ... the marked H tone spreads leftward up to the second mora; other moras receive the default L tone.

sources.citation: Kubozono, Haruo (2006). Where does loanword prosody come from? A case study of Japanese loanword accent. Lingua 116(7), 1140-1170. doi:10.1016/j.lingua.2005.06.010
sources.quote: Most loanwords are known to follow the rule known as 'antepenultimate rule' in (2) if they are lexically accented (McCawley, 1968). ... (2) Loanword accent rule: Put an accent on the syllable containing the antepenultimate mora, or the third mora from the end of the word. ... [p.8:] all three types of words thus described fall into two major accent groups: accented and unaccented. ... Tokyo Japanese further shows a contrast in accent locus for accented nouns. Thus, /í.no.ti/ 'life', /ko.kó.ro/ 'life' and /o.to.kó/ 'man' are accented on the initial, second and final moras, respectively.
sources.note: Lexical accent (presence and locus) in Tokyo Japanese; antepenultimate default for loanwords (93% accented) vs. majority-unaccented native/Sino-Japanese nouns. Confirms the pitch accent coding and the catalog quote's 'accented on the antepenultimate mora'.

sources.citation: Shimabukuro, Moriyo (2002). A reconstruction of the accentual history of the Japanese and Ryukyuan languages. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaii, 411 pp.
sources.quote: in Tokyo Japanese, which is generally considered to be a prototypical pitch-accent language (McCawley 1978), there are two types of nouns: accented and unaccented. In this dissertation the term 'accent' denotes a distinctive fall or rise in pitch ... [p.12:] Tokyo dialect has locus accent, where pitch fall is distinctive, e.g., atama LHH(L) 'head' vs. kokoro LHL(L) 'heart' (Hirayama 1960) ... [p.318:] Tokyo nouns are distinguished by locus only. ... In Tokyo, the initial syllable is always low pitch unless the syllable is accented.
sources.note: Mainly diachronic/comparative, but §6.2.1 gives a synchronic description of Tokyo accent: locus (pitch-fall) accent, accented vs unaccented nouns, initial-lowering; no stress. Confirms the classification.

sources.citation: Okada, Hideo. 1999 [1991]. Japanese. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 117-119. Cambridge: CUP (reprint of JIPA 21(2): 94-96, 1991). Rosetta Project copy, archive.org item rosettaproject_jpn_phon-2.
sources.quote: 'There are two lexically relevant pitch levels: high and low. Within a word, if the first mora is high-pitched, the second is inevitably low-pitched, and vice versa. A mora transcribed with an acute accent ... is said to be accented and is high. ... A word with no accent mark begins low and continues high from the second mora onwards. All moras following the accent are low ...' No stress is described; word prosody is presented purely as lexical pitch accent (speech of educated Tokyo speakers).

sources.citation: Yoshida, Yuko (1995/1999). On pitch accent phenomena in Standard Japanese. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London.
sources.quote: Theoretically, a lexical accent may land on any one of the vowels in a word. However, in Standard Japanese, if a word consists of three 'syllables (in traditional terms)' or less, the lexical accent location is random, unlike longer words whose accent location is predictable (Haraguchi 1991). Also, it is said that there is class of nouns without lexical accent. [...] Note that the pitch pattern is predictable if the location of the accent is known. [...] accent location in certain classes of words is predictable, and accordingly Standard Japanese should be regarded as any other stress system: to wit, the stress (accent) location is predictable, if it is not specified lexically.
